concept.name: Confirmation bias
concept.definition: The tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in ways that confirm one's preexisting beliefs or hypotheses while discounting disconfirming evidence. Documented experimentally since Wason's 1960s work, it operates through biased search, biased interpretation, and biased recall, and is strongest for emotionally charged or deeply held beliefs.
concept.intuition: Once a trader decides the market is going up, every headline starts looking bullish and bearish evidence gets explained away.
concept.mechanics: People prefer 'positive tests' consistent with their working hypothesis, apply stricter evidentiary standards to disconfirming data (disconfirmation bias), and remember congruent evidence more easily; in finance it sustains losing theses and inflates confidence beyond what the evidence supports.
concept.failure_modes: The classic falsification reading has been qualified: a positive-test strategy can be informationally reasonable in some environments (Klayman and Ha), so not every confirmatory search is an error. Belief perseverance can persist even after the original evidence is discredited, corrupting post-trade review.
concept.misconceptions: It is not deliberate dishonesty; the search and interpretation biases are largely automatic. Nor does intelligence protect against it - myside bias appears at all cognitive levels.
concept.example: A long-biased trader reads only bullish analyst notes, treats a revenue miss as already priced in, and recalls only the times the stock rallied on bad news - deepening a losing position.
